# Results — Study 674 (VIDYA)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test —
Tushar Chande's Variable Index Dynamic Average (VIDYA) scales its own smoothing constant
by `|CMO|/100`, so it **speeds up in volatile/trending regimes and slows to a near-freeze
in quiet ones**, beating a fixed-window SMA/EMA — turned into two honest checks: first the
literal mechanism (does `VI = |CMO|/100` actually track realized volatility, and does it
track trend strength — Chande's own pitch conflates the two?), then an honest race: a
VIDYA(14, cmo=9) price-cross long/flat rule vs the same rule on SMA(14) and EMA(14), vs
buy-and-hold, net of one-way costs × NAV, on a five-ticker liquid basket (SPY, QQQ, AAPL,
MSFT, XLE, daily total-return bars). Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last
complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | Rows | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|---|
| SPY  | 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-30 | 8,411  | `40ea383ec57d` |
| QQQ  | 1999-03-10 → 2026-06-30 | 6,869  | `2a5bf2450b6e` |
| AAPL | 1980-12-12 → 2026-06-30 | 11,478 | `997ae710d042` |
| MSFT | 1986-03-13 → 2026-06-30 | 10,152 | `3ee5204493a7` |
| XLE  | 1998-12-22 → 2026-06-30 | 6,921  | `9bee7ba0a5ec` |

Bars are Yahoo daily, **total-return** (`auto_adjust=True` folds splits/dividends into
the close). No survivorship on the Signal axis — these are five large, currently-liquid
tapes (not a "top-N momentum" survivor panel), and the claim under test is about the
*indicator's mechanism*, not a cross-sectional selection.

## The mechanism — does VI actually track volatility, or trend, or neither?

`VIDYA(t) = alpha·VI(t)·P(t) + (1 − alpha·VI(t))·VIDYA(t-1)` with
`VI(t) = |CMO(t, cmo_period)| / 100`. CMO is a pure momentum (net-direction) oscillator —
it reads high when up-moves dominate down-moves over the window, *regardless of how big
the day-to-day swings are*. Chande's pitch says "volatile/trending"; we test both
readings separately (SPY, `cmo_period = 9`):

| Check | Value |
|---|--:|
| corr(VI, trailing 20d realized vol) | **−0.098** (n = 8,391) |
| corr(VI, trailing 20d trend strength, a longer-window CMO) | **+0.380** |
| mean VI, low-volatility tercile → high-volatility tercile | 0.357 → **0.310** |
| mean VI, low-trend tercile → high-trend tercile | 0.261 → **0.446** |

**Volatility half: busted.** VI is *not* higher in high-volatility regimes — if anything
slightly lower (corr −0.10; the high-vol tercile's mean speed knob is *below* the
low-vol tercile's). **Trend half: confirmed.** VI is meaningfully higher when the tape is
trending (corr +0.38; the high-trend tercile runs 71% higher than the low-trend tercile).
Chande's own "volatile" framing is the wrong word for his own formula — the mechanism
tracks *directional persistence*, not *magnitude of movement*.

| Direct check | VIDYA(14, cmo=9) | SMA(14) | EMA(14) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Mean `\|close − line\| / close` (SPY, real tape) | **2.196%** | 1.535% | 1.327% |
| +20% step response: gap closed 5 bars after the shock | **57.6%** | 42.9% | **57.6%** |

The step response confirms the "freeze in quiet, catch up like an EMA in a trend" half of
the mechanism cleanly: before the jump (flat price, CMO ≈ 0) VIDYA does not move at all;
once the sustained jump drives `|CMO|` toward 100, VIDYA's own speed converges to the
*same* catch-up rate as a plain EMA of the same nominal length — VIDYA never *out-runs*
the EMA it's compared to, it just matches it once triggered. But the real-tape tracking
distance runs the other way: VIDYA sits **farther** from price on average than either a
plain SMA or EMA (2.20% vs 1.53%/1.33%) — real markets spend more time in the low-VI
"freeze" state than in the clean, CMO-saturating trend the step test isolates.

## The headline — SPY, net of 5 bps one-way cost

| Rule | Sharpe (net) | CAGR (net) | Max DD | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | switches/yr | time in mkt |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **VIDYA(14, cmo=9)** | **0.387** | **3.68%** | −38.8% | **−3.10** | **−3.54** | **23.1** | 69% |
| SMA(14) cross | 0.238 | 2.07% | −57.6% | −3.70 | −4.42 | 36.5 | 63% |
| EMA(14) cross | 0.267 | 2.40% | −48.0% | −3.57 | −4.22 | 38.3 | 65% |
| **Buy & hold** | **0.647** | **10.83%** | −55.2% | — | — | 0 | 100% |

- All three moving-average timing rules **lose to buy-and-hold**, VIDYA included:
  **−3.10 bps/day at HAC *t* = −3.54**, significant and on the wrong side.
- The **gross** (cost = 0) spread is **−2.64 bps/day, HAC *t* = −3.04** — costs widen the
  hole but are not the root cause; the timing itself is negative.
- VIDYA does have the **shallowest** drawdown of the three rules (−38.8% vs SMA's −57.6%
  and EMA's −48.0%) — the "freeze" state does dodge some chop-driven whipsaw losses — but
  it still trails buy-and-hold's Sharpe by more than a third.

## "Fewer whipsaws than a plain MA?" — the headline claim, measured literally

| Rule | switches/yr (SPY) | vs SMA | vs EMA |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **VIDYA(14, cmo=9)** | **23.1** | **−37%** | **−40%** |
| SMA(14) | 36.5 | — | — |
| EMA(14) | 38.3 | — | — |

Like McGinley Dynamic (Study 672) — and unlike the Hull MA (Study 432, +87% *more*
switches) or KAMA (Study 433, +66% *more* turnover) — **VIDYA genuinely fires fewer
position changes**: 23.1/yr vs the SMA's 36.5 and the EMA's 38.3, a real 37-40% cut, and
the pattern holds basket-wide (see per-instrument table below). The mechanism (freezing
when `|CMO|` is near 0) does what it says on this metric.

## "Beats the plain MA it claims to beat?" — head-to-head

Fewer trades only matters if they are *better* trades. HAC *t* of the VIDYA-minus-SMA and
VIDYA-minus-EMA daily net-return spread (SPY, cost = 5 bps):

| Comparison | spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| VIDYA(14, cmo=9) − SMA(14) | +0.61 | +1.10 |
| VIDYA(14, cmo=9) − EMA(14) | +0.48 | +0.96 |

Positive on paper, on SPY — but **neither clears *t* = 2**. Per-instrument (below),
**zero of 10** such head-to-head comparisons across the five-ticker basket do — a weaker
showing than McGinley Dynamic's 2/10 (Study 672).

## Permutation placebo — is the timing real, or just exposure?

Hold the realised VIDYA position path's block structure but circularly shift it against
returns (destroys the timing, keeps turnover and net-long bias), 2,000 draws, gross
spread statistic:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Observed VIDYA spread | −2.64 bps/day |
| Placebo mean spread | −1.49 bps/day |
| One-sided *p* (placebo ≥ observed) | **0.9885** |

Almost every one of the 2,000 random re-timings beats the real VIDYA calls — the timing
carries **negative** information on this tape, the same failure mode as the desk's other
adaptive-MA teardowns (432, 433, 672, 673).

## Cost sweep (SPY, VIDYA(14, cmo=9))

| round-trip cost | net Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | 0.493 | −2.64 | −3.04 |
| 2.0 bps | 0.450 | −2.82 | −3.24 |
| 5.0 bps | 0.387 | −3.10 | −3.54 |
| 10.0 bps | 0.281 | −3.55 | −4.03 |

The spread is negative before any cost is charged — there is no break-even cost that
rescues it.

## Per-instrument (VIDYA(14, cmo=9) long/flat, cost = 5 bps)

| Ticker | VIDYA Sharpe (net) | Buy&hold Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | V−SMA *t* | V−EMA *t* | switches/yr VIDYA / SMA / EMA |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY  | 0.387 | 0.647 | −3.10 | −3.54 | +1.10 | +0.96 | 23.1 / 36.5 / 38.3 |
| QQQ  | 0.370 | 0.521 | −3.24 | **−2.30** | +0.89 | +0.94 | 24.2 / 36.6 / 39.8 |
| AAPL | 0.742 | 0.623 | −2.17 | −1.21 | +0.62 | +0.27 | 21.6 / 33.1 / 35.7 |
| MSFT | 0.547 | 0.821 | −5.74 | **−4.84** | +0.95 | +0.88 | 22.8 / 37.3 / 40.9 |
| XLE  | 0.238 | 0.428 | −3.18 | **−2.05** | +0.60 | +1.21 | 25.1 / 36.6 / 42.4 |

**Five of five** instruments: the VIDYA timing underperforms buy-and-hold (negative
spread, three of five individually significant at |*t*| ≥ 2 — SPY, QQQ, MSFT, XLE). Against
the plain MAs it claims to beat, **zero of 10** head-to-head comparisons clear *t* = 2 —
positive on paper almost everywhere, certified nowhere.

## Robustness — in/out-of-sample split (SPY, VIDYA(14, cmo=9), cost = 5 bps)

| Half | VIDYA Sharpe (net) | Buy&hold Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| First half (1993–2009) | 0.266 | 0.455 | −2.40 | −1.79 |
| Second half (2009–2026) | 0.540 | 0.872 | −3.71 | **−3.25** |

Negative in **both** halves; the underperformance is not a single-regime artefact.

## Long/short variant (SPY, cost = 5 bps, borrow 50 bps/yr)

Flipping to short when VIDYA is falling makes it worse: net Sharpe **−0.198**, active
spread **−6.23 bps/day** at HAC *t* = **−3.56**. Shorting an upward-drifting index on a
lagging trend signal compounds the loss — the same pattern as McGinley Dynamic's
long/short variant (Study 672).

## CMO-period robustness sweep (SPY, VIDYA period = 14 fixed, cost = 5 bps)

Chande's CMO lookback is a free knob distinct from the base smoothing period; the claim
must survive varying it, not just the one canonical `cmo_period = 9`:

| cmo_period | net Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | switches/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5  | 0.443 | −2.86 | −3.37 | 25.4 |
| 9  | 0.387 | −3.10 | −3.54 | 23.1 |
| 14 | 0.429 | −2.89 | −3.26 | 20.8 |
| 20 | 0.409 | −2.95 | −3.39 | 18.9 |
| 30 | 0.424 | −2.89 | −3.29 | 17.7 |

The active spread is negative and clears *t* ≤ −3.2 at **every** CMO lookback from 5 to
30 bars — the underperformance is not an artefact of the one canonical parameter choice.
Whipsaws fall monotonically as `cmo_period` grows (slower-updating VI freezes more
often), but the Sharpe never approaches buy-and-hold's 0.647 at any setting.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic regime-switching-trend tape (`data.synthetic_panel`, planted-edge knob); no
network.

| World | VIDYA active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | net Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| null (edge = 0), **20 seeds** | — | mean **−0.22** (sd 0.94), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 0/20 seeds** | |
| planted edge = 0.3 (seed 674) | +11.68 | **+9.09** | +2.00 |
| planted edge = 0.6 (seed 674) | +28.69 | **+16.31** | +4.82 |
| planted edge = 1.0 (seed 674) | +50.19 | **+19.82** | +7.48 |

The null never fires across 20 independent streams, and a planted trend lights up hard
and monotonically with its size. *(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in
support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** VIDYA(14, cmo=9) timing's active spread vs buy-and-hold is
  **−3.10 bps/day at HAC *t* = −3.54** on SPY (gross *t* = −3.04), negative on all five
  basket tapes (three of five individually *t* ≤ −2), in both sample halves, at every CMO
  lookback from 5 to 30 bars, and the long/short variant is worse still (*t* = −3.56). The
  permutation placebo gives *p* = 0.9885 — the timing is *worse* than random. The
  volatility-scaled smoothing does not add positive timing information on daily US
  equities.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Net Sharpe 0.387 vs buy-and-hold's 0.647 (gross 0.493, still
  behind); no cost level rescues it, there is no break-even, and the long/short version is
  outright destructive.
- **Speeds up in volatile/trending regimes? — MIXED.** The "trending" half is confirmed
  (corr(VI, trend strength) = +0.38; a deterministic step shows VIDYA freezes in flat
  price and then matches an EMA's catch-up speed once a sustained move saturates CMO).
  The "volatile" half is **busted** (corr(VI, realized vol) = −0.10; the high-volatility
  tercile's mean speed knob is *lower*, not higher, than the low-volatility tercile's).
  Chande's own word for his formula is the wrong one — and even where the mechanism does
  fire honestly (fewer whipsaws, 37-40% below SMA/EMA), it never turns into a certified
  edge over the plain moving averages it claims to beat.
